When a remote service returns `429 Too Many Requests`, honor `Retry-After` if
the selected retry policy supports it. The outbound client's retry behavior and
the inbound response your own API returns are separate decisions.

Not retried: validation errors, authentication/authorization failures, permanent
`404` outcomes, deterministic business rejections, and non-idempotent operations
without a duplicate-prevention strategy.

When a remote endpoint returns `Retry-After`, let the policy follow the server's
guidance instead of an independent aggressive schedule.

## Idempotency

Before retrying a write, ask:

```text
If the first attempt succeeded remotely but the response was lost,
what happens when we send the operation again?
```

If the answer is "duplicate side effect", automatic retry is unsafe. Use an
API-supported idempotency mechanism when appropriate, and do not invent a
client-side `Idempotency-Key` unless the remote service actually supports that
contract.

Avoid retrying every exception or HTTP status, circuit breakers without a failure
scenario, hedging writes, generic resilience wrappers around EF Core without
understanding provider behavior, stacked handlers with overlapping strategies,
and unbounded retry/timeout combinations.

| Scenario | Default consideration |
|---|---|
| External I/O | Bound execution time |
| Safe transient HTTP failure | Consider retry |
| Unsafe write | No retry unless duplicate-safe |
| `429` from dependency | Respect `Retry-After` where appropriate |
| Repeated dependency outage | Consider circuit breaker |
| Optional data unavailable | Consider explicit fallback |
| Latency-sensitive idempotent read | Consider hedging after measurement |
| EF transient faults | Provider/EF execution strategy |
| Incoming request rate limiting | ASP.NET Core rate limiter |

Define consistency semantics first: know how stale data may become and how it is
invalidated. Measure before adding caching solely for performance.

Remove the affected key after a successful mutation; short TTL with tolerated
staleness; tag/group invalidation; versioned keys. Invalidating before the
underlying mutation is known to have succeeded is acceptable only when the
workflow deliberately accepts that behavior.

Application Services perform their normal repository/Unit of Work workflow; if
invalidation is part of the use-case semantics, coordinate it through an
appropriate abstraction. Do not bypass repositories or `IUnitOfWork` to make
invalidation convenient.

## Testing

Test cache behavior when it affects observable correctness: stale entries are
invalidated after a successful mutation; tenant/user keys are isolated; a miss
falls back correctly; an outage follows the intended failure policy. Do not
unit-test framework cache internals.

## Anti-Patterns

Avoid caching EF tracked entities across Unit of Work boundaries, using a cache
as authoritative persistence, and adding Redis merely because the application
has caching.

Review changed data-access and security-sensitive code carefully. When
relevant, check transaction and commit behavior, destructive data changes, raw
SQL parameterization, authorization, input trust boundaries, secrets, sensitive
logging, concurrency, migrations, cache consistency, and — when a migration or
Domain change affects seeded entities — whether `DbSeeder` was reviewed and
updated.

They execute directly against the database and bypass change tracking. Do not
mix them casually with tracked entities representing the same rows, and
understand their transaction and consistency implications.

canonical_policy.name: C# file and async naming conventions remain conventional
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: For new C# code, prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project, normally keep one primary top-level type per matching file, and use the Async suffix for Task/ValueTask-returning methods unless an existing or framework contract makes that inappropriate.

reviews.boundary_analysis: New-code conventions, supporting types and framework-contract exceptions covered; independent BF0007 already records narrower executable async-modifier detection.

context_quotes:
For new C# code, prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the
project, keep one primary top-level type per file by default with the file name
matching that type (small private or nested supporting types may stay with the
owning type), and use the `Async` suffix for methods returning `Task` or
`ValueTask` unless an existing interface or framework contract makes it
inappropriate. Do not rename established APIs solely to add the suffix, and do
not reorganize an existing file merely to satisfy a preferred member ordering.
